Also noteworthy: this commentary says RPM emerges for non-interacting Preisach with a *specific ordering choice* F1+<F2+<... and F1−>F2−>... — the construction orders the up-thresholds ascending and the down-thresholds descending. Hmm! That's the "design" that produces the nested graph with reversibility of order (same order up and down). Interesting: they chose the ordering so the same order holds both ways. But the classical Preisach with arbitrary crossing pairs also has RPM (l-RPM?). Hmm. This is worth noting carefully: maybe for a *discrete* Preisach model, RPM (ordinary, extremal-state-revisiting) holds always, and l-RPM too. Their construction with F1−>F2−>... is just to make the graph look "nested" in an obvious way. Hmm, but for a "crossed" pair, is the graph still l-RPM? Let me check with 2 hysterons: α1 < α2 (1 up first), β1 < β2 (2 down first). Up: 1 then 2. Down: 2 then 1. Graph: 00 →1→ 10 →2→ 11; 11 →2→ 01 →1→ 00. Loops: the "main loop" 00↔11 via 10 (up) and 01 (down). Sub-loops: from 10 down: 1 down at β1 → 00. So loop {10,00}: absorbing. From 01 up: 2 up at α2 → 11. So it's fine. l-RPM requires loops be absorbing: consider the loop between 00 and 11 with up-boundary {10} and down-boundary {01}: from 10 (an up-boundary), can we reach 11 by up transitions? 10→11 by 2 up: yes. From 01 (down boundary) can we reach 00 by down transitions? 01 → 00 by 1 down: yes. So absorbing. Fine. So l-RPM holds. Good: crossed Preisach is still l-RPM. So my "constructed counterexample" (orders differ between halves but RPM holds) is fine, and more strongly: published construction notes the same order in both halves is a *choice* ("Due to the choice of ordering the F_i−, this will be also the same order in which the elements return"), implying that with a different choice the return order differs yet the device still records history. Good — that supports my correction: a single state-independent ordering is not required.
